accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE statutory RSHE guidance (2019, updated 2025) for primary Mental wellbeing: pupils should know how to recognise and talk about their emotions, that feelings can be shown in different ways, and how to seek support from a trusted adult. Display rules follow Ekman and Friesen; masking and non-verbal cues (facial expression, body language, tone of voice) match the PSHE Association Health and wellbeing strand for KS2.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets both literal and over-suspicious readings: prediction 1 offers Yes, she said so (tag words), Raj's matching clues are judged really fine and the always tag corrects anyone who thinks every smile is a mask. Secret-keeping after being hurt (tags hide and wait) is corrected with tell a trusted grown-up, and public call-outs (tags liar and class) are corrected with a private, gentle check-in.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagmask uses a draggable magnifier that reveals face, body and voice clues on three drawn friends, a smile mask the child drags upward to expose the real expression, two reason and keep-or-share card sorts and an ordered check-in builder with decoys. Bystanders (flagupst), Everyday kindness (flagcare) and feelings labs do not use clue inspection or masks, and the shingle gate passed against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Driving the lab: the child cannot judge a friend until all three clues are seen, so the rule check face, body and voice is enforced by the interaction. Bea's fists and Ola's floor gaze contrast with Raj, whose clues all match, so the matching-clues idea is discovered by comparison. Lifting Mia, Leo and Ada's masks shows a different face before naming the feeling, and done messages state the rule after the rounds.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong answers the lab then tests: Ola is fine because she said so (the magnifier shows her clues disagree), Leo is happy because he is laughing (the lifted mask shows hurt), and Rae should keep hiding two weeks of sadness (the keep-or-share sort puts long feelings with a trusted grown-up). A.reveal quotes the child's guess in each done message.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Four rotating challenge questions with eight tagged wrong answers, each with its own fix in because(): words, rude, always, acting, hide, wait, liar and class. In-lab slips also explain, for example judging Raj not fine says his face, body and voice match the words, and putting a hurt secret in keep private says hurting is never a secret to keep.

readability.evidence: Kid text is under the family kid grade limit with short sentences a parent can read aloud (A smile can be like a mask. Inside he feels hurt.). Adult text stays under the family adult limit while naming emotional literacy, masking, non-verbal cues, facial expression, body language, tone of voice, display rules, empathy, RSHE Mental wellbeing and IB PYP PSPE.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed and explanation overlap with Naming feelings, Bystanders and Upstanders and Everyday Kindness is under 12 percent. Each kid paragraph does one job (words versus clues, the mask idea, why people hide, keep or share), and the adult paragraphs give the curriculum home, a glossary, named mistakes with a safeguarding caution, and the lab outline.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px Android dark and iPhone 13 light: the friend figure and three question-mark spots are large enough to drag the magnifier with a thumb, the smile mask and its stick clear the face, the reason and keep-or-share cards are full-width rows with three tall bins, and the check-in options wrap to two lines without clipping in either theme.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark on desktop and iPhone 13, no console or page errors, all Show me tasks completed and the challenge rendered. Every drag has a button twin (Check the face, body or voice; Lift the mask; Pick a card and Put in each box; each check-in step), and the canvas aria-label speaks each clue and result.
